Yes, such a function and sequence exist. Here is the proof.

**Construction.** Define $f:\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}$ by
$$f(x)=\frac{1}{x^{2}-2}.$$

**Well-definedness and continuity.** For every $x\in\mathbb{Q}$, we have $x^{2}\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $x^{2}-2\in\mathbb{Q}$. Since $x^{2}=2$ has no rational solution (as $\sqrt{2}\notin\mathbb{Q}$), the denominator $x^{2}-2\neq 0$, so $f(x)\in\mathbb{Q}$. Thus $f$ is well-defined as a map $\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}$.

For continuity: fix any $x_{0}\in\mathbb{Q}$. The polynomial $g(x)=x^{2}-2$ is continuous at $x_{0}$, and $g(x_{0})=x_{0}^{2}-2\neq 0$. The function $h(y)=1/y$ is continuous at every nonzero $y_{0}$. Since $f=h\circ g$ and $g(x_{0})\neq 0$, $f$ is continuous at $x_{0}$. As $x_{0}$ was arbitrary, $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{Q}$.

**The Cauchy sequence.** Let $x_{n}=\frac{\lfloor \sqrt{2}\cdot 10^{n}\rfloor}{10^{n}}$. Each $x_{n}$ is rational, and $x_{n}\to\sqrt{2}$ in $\mathbb{R}$, so $\{x_{n}\}$ is convergent in $\mathbb{R}$, hence Cauchy in $\mathbb{R}$, hence Cauchy in $\mathbb{Q}$.

**The image is not Cauchy.** Since $x_{n}\to\sqrt{2}$, by continuity of $x\mapsto x^{2}$ we have $x_{n}^{2}\to 2$, so $x_{n}^{2}-2\to 0$. Therefore
$$|f(x_{n})|=\frac{1}{|x_{n}^{2}-2|}\to+\infty.$$
The sequence $\{f(x_{n})\}$ is unbounded. Every Cauchy sequence (in any metric space) is bounded, so $\{f(x_{n})\}$ is **not** Cauchy.

**$f$ is not uniformly continuous.** A standard theorem states that every uniformly continuous function maps Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences. We have exhibited a Cauchy sequence $\{x_{n}\}$ in $\mathbb{Q}$ whose image $\{f(x_{n})\}$ is not Cauchy. By contrapositive, $f$ is not uniformly continuous on $\mathbb{Q}$.

**Conclusion.** The function $f(x)=1/(x^{2}-2)$ is continuous $\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}$, is not uniformly continuous, and the Cauchy sequence $x_{n}=\lfloor\sqrt{2}\cdot 10^{n}\rfloor/10^{n}$ of rationals has image $\{f(x_{n})\}$ that is unbounded and hence not Cauchy. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
